archetype.name: Pocket Passer (volume-driven)
archetype.definition: A second-year, 6-foot-5 rotation-and-throw passer whose value comes from steady volume and a productive intermediate-to-deep game, with enough scramble ability to punish loose rushes but no real designed-run threat.

report.headline: Volume carries Shough; the downfield game works, the screens and third downs don't
report.take:
Shough's season looks like a top-15 quarterback in the box score and a league-average one under the hood. He is averaging 248.3 passing yards a game (13th of 49) on a pace for 4220 yards and 30 touchdowns, but his 0.009 EPA per dropback ranks 27th and his 6.45 yards per attempt ranks 34th, below the qualifier average of 6.89. The volume isn't a scheme forcing the ball through him: New Orleans passes almost exactly as often as situation predicts (-0.2 over expected). It comes from games that stay live because the Saints' defense can't stop anything deep. They allow the worst deep-pass EPA in the league, which is how you get a 30-31 opener and a 24-45 loss to Atlanta.

The shape of his passing is the real story. On throws of 10+ air yards he is at 0.364 EPA per attempt, and the intermediate (0.359) and deep (0.371) buckets are both strong. Chris Olave (0.447 EPA per target) and Devaughn Vele (0.403) are the engine. The bleed is underneath. Throws behind the line have cost 20.2 EPA in total at -0.421 per attempt, which wipes out most of what the short game adds and leaves everything under 10 air yards at just 0.031 a play. Bryce Lance's 24 targets at -0.559 EPA each are a second drain. Shough has also pushed the ball more this year: aggressiveness is up 3.8 points from his rookie season. His biggest growth is in the pocket. His pressure-to-sack rate fell from 41.9% last year, 48th of 62, to 24.6% (14th of 42), and his bad-throw rate dropped 1.7 points.

What the season line hides is where drives die. On third down he is at -0.207 EPA a play, converting 37.1% against an average of 8 yards to go, and 10 of his 20 sacks have come there. His accuracy has also slid. CPOE is down 2.4 from last season and sits at -5.1 over the last three games, including a -17.2 at the Giants that three touchdowns papered over. Ball security is a real flaw, not just bad luck. He has three lost fumbles (45th of 49) and eight turnover-worthy fumbles in eight games. The red zone has been his best area: 12 touchdowns on 39 attempts with a CPOE of 10.4. Under-center work (0.209 EPA on 46 plays) has also outperformed shotgun (-0.053), a small-sample hint the staff could lean on.

From here, expect a high floor on volume and wide swings on efficiency, driven largely by the opponent. He posted -11.9 EPA against Minnesota, the league's top defense, but +10.6 against sixth-ranked Pittsburgh when he went quick and short. So the swings track the plan as much as the opponent. Losing center Erik McCoy, a 97%-snap starter, for "a little bit" is the near-term headwind, landing right where his weakness already lives: obvious passing downs against interior pressure.

strengths.title: Real production beyond ten yards
strengths.body: His 10+ air-yard throws are producing 0.364 EPA per attempt, and both the intermediate and deep buckets are well above his overall rate. That comes from a real connection with Olave and Vele and a willingness to push the ball that grew from last season. It should hold, because it rests on his two best receivers and a trait that has strengthened year over year.

strengths.title: Pocket management has grown up
strengths.body: His pressure-to-sack rate dropped from 41.9% as a rookie, among the worst, to 24.6% this year, middle-of-the-pack or better. His bad-throw rate improved too. When he does escape, he gains value: 0.77 EPA per scramble, with 8 first downs on 14 scrambles. This looks like genuine second-year development rather than noise, though McCoy's absence will test it.

strengths.title: Finishing in the red zone
strengths.body: Twelve of his 14 touchdown passes have come inside the 20, on 71.8% completions and a 10.4 CPOE, which is the single best accuracy split on his card. Some regression in that CPOE is likely on 39 attempts. His overall touchdown rate is only 25th, though, so the scoring isn't inflated luck.

concerns.title: Third downs and the screen game
concerns.body: On third down he is at -0.207 EPA a play, with half his sacks coming there, and throws behind the line have cost more than 20 EPA in total. Those two areas are why a strong downfield profile nets out near league average. The screens are partly a design and personnel issue (Lance's targets are a big negative), but the third-down struggles fall on him.

concerns.title: Ball security is a genuine flaw
concerns.body: He has three lost fumbles, ranking 45th of 49, and eight turnover-worthy fumbles in eight games. The lost total could regress a bit with bounce luck, but the underlying fumble count says he is loose with the ball in the pocket. With a backup center now snapping and blocking, it is not likely to fix itself.

concerns.title: Accuracy has slipped
concerns.body: CPOE is down 2.4 from his rookie year and at -5.1 over the last three games, even as EPA recovered. The recent EPA bump is riding big plays and touchdowns more than consistent placement. Yards per attempt is also down 0.84 from last year, so the more aggressive approach hasn't yet paid off in efficiency.

trend.note: Game EPA has swung from +10.9 at Baltimore to -11.9 against Minnesota and back to +10.6 against Pittsburgh. His last three games beat his season rate by 0.063 EPA per dropback, but with worse accuracy, so the upswing is fragile.

nextGame.headline: Carolina can't rush the passer and is missing its corners
nextGame.body:
Carolina's defense ranks 22nd in EPA and 23rd against the pass. It is dead last in both sack rate and QB hit rate, which goes straight at Shough's main pressure and third-down problems. The catch is that the Panthers rank 2nd in limiting explosive passes and allow just 0.09 EPA per target to opposing WR1s (4th), so Olave may get capped and the yards may have to come in chunks of 10 to 19 rather than shots. Tight ends have feasted on them, which points to Juwan Johnson. Carolina's own offense passes far more than expected (3rd), and New Orleans gives up the worst deep EPA in the league, so a live, back-and-forth script near the 47.5 total is plausible. The game is indoors, and the Saints are 1.5-point favorites.

Availability tilts toward Shough. Carolina is without corners Will Lee III (out) and Jaycee Horn and Mike Jackson (both on IR), plus linebackers Bobby Okereke and Jaelan Phillips, gutting the coverage and removing a rusher from a unit that already gets no pressure. On his side, center Erik McCoy is listed questionable, but Kellen Moore says he'll miss "a little bit," so expect a backup at center and more interior leakage than usual. The backfield is also thin, with Travis Etienne on IR and CJ Donaldson out, which leaves a heavier load on Alvin Kamara, whose targets have been neutral at best.

keyMatchups.title: Toothless rush versus missing center
keyMatchups.body: Carolina has the league's lowest sack and hit rates, and it is without Phillips. That should offset much of the McCoy loss and give Shough clean third-down looks, where he has struggled most. If the backup center gets beaten anyway, the third-down sack problem resurfaces.

keyMatchups.title: Depleted corners, but explosives capped
keyMatchups.body: With three corners down, the intermediate and deep throws that drive his efficiency should be there. Carolina, however, has been among the best at preventing explosive passes and at limiting WR1s. That makes Vele and the 10-to-19-yard window more likely winners than Olave shots.

keyMatchups.title: Tight end soft spot
keyMatchups.body: Carolina allows 0.4 EPA per tight-end target, 26th in the league, and lets TE1s beat their averages. Juwan Johnson has been productive at 0.297 EPA per target, so this is where Shough's short game can finally add value instead of bleeding it.

nextGame.watch: Whether he converts third downs with a backup center against the league's weakest pass rush. If he can't here, it's a real trait, not the protection.

restOfSeason.body:
The volume is the sustainable part: he has started every game and plays essentially every snap. A defense that leaks deep plays keeps games open, so something in the 225 to 270 passing-yard range is a fair weekly expectation. His downfield efficiency and improved sack avoidance look like real second-year growth. The red-zone accuracy and the touchdown bursts in weeks like the Giants game are likelier to cool, and the 1.3 to 1.9 touchdown range reflects that. Rushing should sit around 15 to 28 yards a game, built on scrambles rather than designed runs, which have been stuffed almost half the time.

The ceiling depends on fixing the two leaks: the screen game and third downs. If the staff trims the negative touches underneath and leans on the under-center looks that have worked, his efficiency could climb toward the top half. If not, he stays a 15 to 20 PPR-point volume passer with a few disaster games against good defenses. The fumbles will keep costing real points either way until his ball security improves.
swingFactors: Whether the screen game and Bryce Lance's targets get trimmed

confidence.note: Eight starts with large game-to-game swings, a new center, and only one prior season for career context.
